newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian PM urges patience in hostage rescue.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian PM urges patience in hostage rescue.

text.p: First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh on Thursday urged patience in the jungle search for Briton Christopher Howes, who was abducted eight months ago in northern Cambodia.

"We have to face realities. The area has a lot of forests...and floods, and we dare not use radios because that is very dangerous," Ranariddh told reporters, adding he knew the area from his days with the 1980s anti-Vietnamese resistance against the Hanoi-backed government in Phnom Penh.

He said the government had heard Khmer Rouge radio transmissions that indicated hardline guerrillas were trying to recapture mines clearance expert Howes, 37, and his Cambodian interpreter Houn Hourth, who are believed to have escaped from the rebel base of Anlong Veng near the Thai border.
The government on Wednesday dispatched troops to Phnom (Mountain) Chan, an area that borders territory controlled by hardline Khmer Rouge rebels, in hopes of making contact with the two men.
The mountain, located about 200 km (125 miles) north of Phnom Penh in the province of Preah Vihear, is the third of three possible meeting points which had been set up by a Khmer Rouge go-between.
The two hostages, who government officials say are accompanied by a group of 140 dissident Khmer Rouge who helped them flee, have not showed at the other two meeting sites.
"We have to wait and be patient and let the people there do their job," Ranariddh said, adding that he urged media responsibility in reporting the case.
"(If) we start to talk too much about it, it is not good for (Howes)," he told reporters.
But Ranariddh said he remained optimistic about the fate of the two men.
Howes and Houn Hourth were abducted on March 26 while conducting mines clearance work in the northern province of Siem Reap.
The two men were reported to have escaped with a group of Khmer Rouge dissidents last week, but reports of their freedom remain unconfirmed.

The Khmer Rouge, which led the genocidal 1975-1979 "killing fields" regime, have been decimated by thousands of defections in recent months, but a group of 800 to 2,000 hardliners are estimated to remain in the Anlong Veng area.
